59: 60:# 4. Byte-Pair Encoding, step by step 61: 62:With the stakes clear, the algorithm itself turns out to be almost disappointingly simple, which is a good sign. Byte-Pair Encoding is a loop you could run on a whiteboard. You begin by treating every word as a sequence of single characters. You count every adjacent pair of symbols across the whole corpus, weighted by how often each word appears. You find the single most frequent pair and merge it into one new token, and you write that merge down in an ordered list. Then you repeat the count and the merge and the record, again and again, until the vocabulary reaches the size you were aiming for. That is the entire training procedure. 63: 64:Two artifacts come out of this loop, and it is worth naming them clearly because everything later depends on them. The first artifact is the vocabulary, which is simply the set of tokens that now exist. The second artifact is the ordered list of merges, which is the set of rules. The rules are ordered for a reason, because to tokenize a brand new piece of text you replay exactly these merges in exactly this order, and the order is what makes the result deterministic. If you watch a tiny corpus go through three or four merges, you can see related words such as "low" and "lower" and "lowest" come to share the same early merges, which is the precise moment the middle path stops being an idea and becomes a mechanism. 65: 66: 67: 68: 69:> A clean step-through of the core loop, advancing one merge at a time so you can watch characters fuse into larger and larger tokens while the merge list grows beside them. 70: 71:

Instead of merging the pair that is simply most frequent, it merges the pair that most increases the likelihood of the corpus, which is a way of preferring pairs whose two halves travel together far more often than chance would predict. # Session 2: Tokenization and Vocabulary Design
# 1. What this session is Session 1 closed on a single promise, which is that **words have to become numbers** before any neural network can begin to work on them, and that the first step in turning words into numbers is a step called **tokenization**. Tokenization is the place where raw human text is chopped into the units that the model will actually see, and the way you perform that chopping quietly determineds the **cost**, the **fairness**, and even the **basic spelling ability** of every model trained on top of it. The plan for the session is to begin with the problem rather than the solution, so that every technique we introduce arrives as the answer to a difficulty we'll face. We will build up from the two obvious and broken ways of splitting text, discover subword tokenization as the middle path, learn the Byte-Pair Encoding algorithm as a loop you could run by hand, and then widen out to the family of related algorithms you will choose between when you build your own. From there we look at vocabulary size as a real engineering dial, at a frequency-sorted identifier scheme that came directly out of the V4 BrahmicTokenizer work, at the precise seam where tokenization ends and the embedding table begins, and finally at the Indic-script challenges that make this work a… The real objective of today is not to have you reproduce an existing tokenizer. It is to equip you to design your own and to defend the choices behind it, which is exactly what the closing hands-on exercise asks you to do.
# 2. The dilemma before the algorithm Before we reach for any algorithm, it is worth feeling the problem that the algorithm exists to solve. Take a single sentence and try to split it in the two most obvious ways. The first way is to split it into individual characters, which gives you a tiny set of symbols to learn, since a couple of hundred characters cover most of English. The cost of that choice is that sequences become enormous, and the model spends a large part of its capacity rediscovering, over and over again, that the three characters t, h, and e tend to travel together as the word "the." The second way is to split the sentence into whole words, which gives you short sequences that are pleasant to work with. The cost of that choice is that the vocabulary explodes without limit, every ty…
The question that this tension plants is the one that the rest of the session answers. Is there a middle path that keeps the common things whole and breaks only the rare things into pieces? That middle path exists, it is called subword tokenization, and **Byte-Pair Encoding** is one well-known way to find it. Everything that follows is built on top of this felt problem, so it is worth spending real time here until the trade-off feels obvious rather than abstract. > Goal: you should leave feeling, rather than just being told, that neither extreme is workable and that something in between is needed.
# 3. Why tokenization is load-bearing Now that the trade-off is in your hands, it is worth making the stakes explicit, because tokenization is unusual among the decisions in a training pipeline. It is decided exactly once, before training begins, and everything downstream inherits it permanently. The length of every sequence, and therefore the compute spent on every sentence, is fixed by it. The set of things the model is even capable of spelling is fixed by it, because a string that never became a token has no symbol the model can ever produce. The fairness of the model across different languages is fixed by it. And the size of the embedding table, which is one of the largest single pieces of the whole model, is fixed by it. You cannot repair a bad tokenizer by training for longer, in the same … The clearest way to feel the cost is through the bill. Suppose your tokenizer splits Telugu into roughly three times as many tokens as it uses for the same meaning in English. Every Telugu user then pays close to three times the inference cost for the same request, and the model sees only about a third as much Telugu context inside the same fixed window. This is not a rounding error and it does not heal with scale, because a larger context window lifts both languages together and leaves the ratio between them untouched. This is the natural place for the Indic-script motivation to enter the session, not as a footnote at the end but as a direct consequence of a single early decision. > A view of the tokenizer as a frozen decision, with a set of presets that lean the tokenizer toward characters, toward English words, or toward a balanced subword scheme, and a panel that traces how each downstream property changes as a result.

# 4. Byte-Pair Encoding, step by step With the stakes clear, the algorithm itself turns out to be almost disappointingly simple, which is a good sign. Byte-Pair Encoding is a loop you could run on a whiteboard. You begin by treating every word as a sequence of single characters. You count every adjacent pair of symbols across the whole corpus, weighted by how often each word appears. You find the single most frequent pair and merge it into one new token, and you write that merge down in an ordered list. Then you repeat the count and the merge and the record, again and again, until the vocabulary reaches the size you were aiming for. That is the entire training procedure. Two artifacts come out of this loop, and it is worth naming them clearly because everything later depends on them. The first artifact is the vocabulary, which is simply the set of tokens that now exist. The second artifact is the ordered list of merges, which is the set of rules. The rules are ordered for a reason, because to tokenize a brand new piece of text you replay exactly these merges in exactly this order, and the order is what makes the result deterministic. WordPiece keeps almost the whole structure of Byte-Pair Encoding but changes the rule for which pair to merge. Instead of merging the pair that is simply most frequent, it merges the pair that most increases the likelihood of the corpus, which is a way of preferring pairs whose two halves travel together far more often than chance would predict. The practical effect is a gentle bias toward subwords that feel meaningful, so that a tightly bound pair can win a merge even when a more common but less cohesive pair exists. Kronecker factorization is an embedding-side trick, not a tokenization trick, and it lives on the far side of the seam from everything else in this…

The Indic-script deep dive Now that you have the full vocabulary of ideas from the rest of the session, the Indic-script problems can be pulled into one focused block, because you finally have the language to understand why they are hard. Scripts such as Devanagari, Telugu, Bengali, and Odia are not simply English written with different letters. They carry conjunct consonants, where several consonants fuse into a single written cluster. They use joiner characters, the zero-width joiner and the zero-width non-joiner, which are invisible on the page yet carry real meaning and change what the correct token boundaries are. This is where the dial stops being a tokenizer question and becomes an architecture question. At the 131K vocabulary used in the V4 BrahmicTokenizer, paired with a model width of 8096, the embedding table alone holds on the order of a billion parameters, which is already larger than many complete models and occupies a couple of gigabytes before a single transformer layer has been added. At that size, the question is no longer only which tokens to include. It becomes the question of how you are going to store this matrix at all, and that question is the deliberate hand-off into the seam we look at next. > An interactive dial where you slide the vocabulary size and watch the two ends of the trade-off move in opposite directions, the sequence length and compute on one side and the embedding table on the other, while a parameter breakdown shows the tables quietly taking over the model at smaller scales. A hand-off panel reports the size of the table at the 131K setting and points directly at the storage problem.
# 7. The seam, from token IDs to embeddings, and where Kronecker lives It helps to be very precise about where one layer ends and the next begins, because a lot of confusion in this area comes from blurring the boundary. The tokenizer's entire job is finished the moment text has become a sequence of integer identifiers. Nothing about the tokenizer says what those integers mean as vectors. The very next question, which is what vector each identifier turns into, belongs to a different component entirely, which is the embedding table. Keeping these two layers separate in your mind is important, because it tells you exactly which kinds of fixes belong on which side of the seam. The storage problem we set up in the previous section lives entirely on the embedding side of this seam. A dense embedding table at 131K by 8096 is enormous, and one way to tame it is to stop storing it densely. **Kronecker factorization** represents that single large table as the Kronecker product of two much smaller matrices, which reconstructs a table of the same shape while storing only a tiny fraction of the parameters. This is the technique that the V4 work released openly under an Apache 2.0 license, on the strength of how unusual it is. For today the important thing is not the mechanics but the placement. Kronecker factorization is an embedding-side trick, not a tokenization trick, and it lives on the far side of the seam from everything else in this…
# 8. The Indic-script deep dive Now that you have the full vocabulary of ideas from the rest of the session, the Indic-script problems can be pulled into one focused block, because you finally have the language to understand why they are hard. Scripts such as Devanagari, Telugu, Bengali, and Odia are not simply English written with different letters. They carry conjunct consonants, where several consonants fuse into a single written cluster. They use joiner characters, the zero-width joiner and the zero-width non-joiner, which are invisible on the page yet carry real meaning and change what the correct token boundaries are. They attach vowel signs, the matras, onto consonants, and a naive tokenizer will happily slice through the middle of one of these grapheme clusters. On top of all of th… In Hindi, several consonants can combine into one visual unit called a **संयुक्ताक्षर** or conjunct consonant. For example: ```text क् + ष = क्ष त् + र = त्र ज् + ञ = ज्ञ श् + र = श्र ``` The symbol `्` is the **halant/virama**. It removes the inherent vowel from a consonant. Normally: ```text क = ka क् = k ष = ṣa क् + ष = क्ष ``` Although `क्ष` may look like one character, Unicode stores it as multiple code points: ```text क + ् + ष ``` This matters to tokenizers. A tokenizer that splits by visible glyphs may treat `क्ष` as one unit, while a tokenizer operating on Unicode code points sees three components. ## Hindi example: शक्ति The word: ```text शक्ति ``` contains the conjunct `क्त`: ```text श + क् + त + ि ``` Visually, `क्` and `त` combine into `क्त`. A tokenizer should ideally avoid breaking the word at an arbitrary point inside this sequence, such as: ```text शक | ् | ति ``` A better segmentation might preserve the conjunct: ```text श | क्ति ``` or preserve useful linguistic pieces: ```text शक्ति ``` ## Zero-width joiner and non-joiner Hindi text can also contain invisible Unicode characters: * **ZWJ:** zero-width joiner, `U+200D` * **ZWNJ:** zero-width non-joiner, `U+200C` They are placed around the halant to influence how consonants are rendered. ### Normal conjunct ```text क + ् + ष ``` Usually renders as: ```text क्ष ``` ### With ZWNJ ```text क + ् + ZWNJ + ष ``` This requests that the consonants remain visually separate: ```text क्‌ष ``` The halant may remain visible rather than forming the `क्ष` ligature. ### With ZWJ ```text क + ् + ZWJ + ष ``` … …

content.text:
I've got the full walkthrough. Here's the widget's tiny corpus and complete BPE trace, then the explanation.

## The widget's setup

**Tiny weighted corpus:** `low×5, lower×2, lowest×1, newer×1, wider×1`

Start state: every word is just its raw characters, and pair counts are tallied (weighted by word frequency):

```
l+o: 8   o+w: 8   e+r: 4   w+e: 4   d+e: 1   e+s: 1   e+w: 1   i+d: 1   n+e: 1
```

(`l+o` and `o+w` both hit 8 because `low` appears 5 times and `l-o-w` is a prefix shared by `lower`(×2) and `lowest`(×1) too → 5+2+1=8 each.)

## Step-by-step merges

| Step | Winning pair | New token | Why it wins |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `l + o` | `lo` | tied at 8, alphabetically/arbitrarily first |
| 2 | `lo + w` | `low` | now `lo+w` is the new count-8 leader |
| 3 | `e + r` | `er` | `er` appears in `lower`(×2) + `newer`(×1) + `wider`(×1) = 4 |
| 4 | `low + er` | `lower` | after step 3, `low` (from step 2) directly precedes `er` in the word "lower" |

Each merge is **recorded in order** into the merge list:
```
1. l + o → lo
2. lo + w → low
3. e + r → er
4. low + er → lower
```

## Encoding new text (replay, don't re-search)

The widget shows this directly: to tokenize a brand-new word like `lower`, you don't recompute anything — you just **replay the merge rules in the order they were learned**:

```
start:            l o w e r
apply rule 1 (l+o→lo):   lo w e r
apply rule 2 (lo+w→low): low e r
apply rule 3 (e+r→er):   low er
(rule 4 low+er→lower doesn't apply here in this widget's trace — 
 final shown encoding is "lo · w · e · r"... )
```

Actually the widget's own final line for encoding `lower` says: **`Final encoded form: lo · w · e · r`** — i.e., it stopped applying rules after rule 1 in that particular encode-demo panel, showing that if you only had 1 merge rule learned so far, `lower` would tokenize as `lo, w, e, r`. This is the widget deliberately showing an *intermediate* state of the tokenizer (only 1 rule learned) being applied to new text — not the fully-trained 4-rule tokenizer.

## Explaining BPE from this example

1. **Init**: treat text as raw characters — the entire "vocabulary" starts as just the alphabet used (`d,e,i,l,n,o,r,s,t,w` here).
2. **Count**: tally every adjacent symbol pair across the whole corpus, weighting by how many times each word occurs (`low` counts 5×, not 1×).
3. **Merge**: take the single most frequent pair, fuse it into one new symbol, add it to the vocabulary.
4. **Record**: append the merge to an ordered rule list — order matters because it's replayed later.
5. **Repeat**: go back to counting (pair frequencies shift after every merge — e.g. once `lo` exists, `l+o` disappears from future counts and `lo+w` becomes the new candidate).
6. **Stop** once vocab hits your target size.
7. **Encoding new/unseen text**: apply the *same* learned rules in the *same order* — no retraining, no search. This is why BPE is deterministic and fast at inference time, and why merge **order** is one of the two artifacts you must ship (the other being the vocab itself).

The key insight the widget is built to make visceral: `low`, `lower`, `lowest` **share early merges** (`l+o`, `lo+w`) because they share a prefix — that shared structure is exactly what lets a fixed-size vocabulary generalize to related words instead of needing a separate token for every whole word.
what is the input sequence

In the widget's "Encoding new text" panel, the **input sequence being encoded is the word `lower`**.

Trace shown:
```
start from characters:  l  o  w  e  r
apply rule 1 (l + o → lo):   lo  w  e  r
```

That's the word from the corpus (`lower×2`) chosen specifically because it shares a prefix (`low`) with the more frequent `low×5` and `lowest×1` — so you can watch it reuse the early merges (`l+o`, `lo+w`) rather than needing brand-new rules of its own.

Want me to step through the full 4-rule replay on `lower` (rather than the widget's partial 1-rule snapshot) to show the complete final tokenization?
what is the corpus

## The corpus

The widget uses a **tiny, hand-picked, frequency-weighted corpus** of 5 words:

| Word | Frequency |
|---|---:|
| `low` | ×5 |
| `lower` | ×2 |
| `lowest` | ×1 |
| `newer` | ×1 |
| `wider` | ×1 |

That's it — just 5 word *types*, but with counts attached so the algorithm has real frequencies to work with (this is the classic toy example from the original Sennrich et al. BPE paper, slightly adapted).

**Why these 5 words specifically:**
- `low`, `lower`, `lowest` all share the prefix `l-o-w` → shows how BPE merges (`l+o`, `lo+w`) get **reused** across related words
- `lower`, `newer`, `wider` all share the suffix `e-r` → shows a second, independent merge (`e+r → er`) emerging from a different shared pattern
- `lower` sits at the intersection of both patterns, which is why it's the word chosen for the "encode new text" demo — it needs *both* learned rules to fully tokenize

The weighting (`low×5`) matters because BPE counts pairs **weighted by word frequency**, not just unique word types — that's exactly why `l+o` and `o+w` start out tied at count 8 (5 from `low` + 2 from `lower` + 1 from `lowest`).
alright so what do we do first. collect frequency of all the adjacent pairs?

Yes, exactly.

## Step 1: Count adjacent pairs (frequency table)

Start with every word broken into raw characters, then tally **every adjacent pair**, weighted by how often each word occurs.

For this corpus:

| Word | Frequency | Characters | Adjacent pairs |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `low` | ×5 | `l o w` | `l-o`, `o-w` |
| `lower` | ×2 | `l o w e r` | `l-o`, `o-w`, `w-e`, `e-r` |
| `lowest` | ×1 | `l o w e s t` | `l-o`, `o-w`, `w-e`, `e-s`, `s-t` |
| `newer` | ×1 | `n e w e r` | `n-e`, `e-w`, `w-e`, `e-r` |
| `wider` | ×1 | `w i d e r` | `w-i`, `i-d`, `d-e`, `e-r` |

Now tally each pair, multiplying by word frequency:

```
l+o: 5(low) + 2(lower) + 1(lowest)              = 8
o+w: 5(low) + 2(lower) + 1(lowest)              = 8
w+e: 2(lower) + 1(lowest) + 1(newer)            = 4
e+r: 2(lower) + 1(newer) + 1(wider)             = 4
d+e: 1(wider)                                    = 1
e+s: 1(lowest)                                   = 1
```

## The merge process, mechanically

"Merging a pair" means: take two adjacent symbols that always appear next to each other in this instance, and **glue them into one new symbol** that the algorithm now treats as a single, atomic unit going forward.

Concretely, for merge 1 (`l + o → lo`), here's what happens step by step:

### 1. Scan every word in the corpus for the winning pair
Look at each word's current symbol sequence and find every place where `l` is immediately followed by `o`.

```
low     → l o w        found "l,o" at position 0-1
lower   → l o w e r    found "l,o" at position 0-1
lowest  → l o w e s t  found "l,o" at position 0-1
newer   → n e w e r    no "l,o" here — untouched
wider   → w i d e r    no "l,o" here — untouched
```

### 2. Replace every matched pair with the new merged symbol
Wherever `l` and `o` sit adjacent, collapse those two symbols into one token `lo`. Everything else in the word stays as-is.

```
l o w        → lo w
l o w e r    → lo w e r
l o w e s t  → lo w e s t
```

### 3. Add the new symbol to the vocabulary
`lo` didn't exist before. It's now a first-class token, just like `l`, `o`, `w`, etc. were.

```
vocab: {d, e, i, l, n, o, r, s, t, w}  →  {d, e, i, l, n, o, r, s, t, w, lo}
```

### 4. Record the rule in the ordered merge list
This is the part that makes the merge **reusable later** — you don't just change the corpus, you also write down *how* you got there.

```
merge list: [ ]  →  [ "l + o → lo" ]
```

### 5. Re-tally pair counts on the new board
Because `l` and `o` no longer exist separately inside those words (they're fused into `lo`), the adjacency structure changed. `o+w` (count 8 before) effectively disappears — it's now `lo+w`, a brand new pair to count in the next round.

```
lo + w : 8   (was tracked as o+w before)
w + e  : 4
e + r  : 4
... etc
```

That re-tallied table is what step 2 will pick a winner from.

### Why this matters
A merge does two things at once:
- **Mutates the corpus representation** (shorter symbol sequences, since `lo` replaces two symbols with one)
- **Mutates the rule book** (the merge list), which is the artifact that lets you apply the *exact same transformation* to brand-new, unseen text later — that's the "replay" step in encoding.

Nothing is merged "everywhere in the abstract alphabet" — it's merged **only where that specific adjacency actually occurs** in the data. If `l` appeared next to `x` somewhere, that instance is untouched; only `l` next to `o` gets fused.

## The convention in this widget: pre-split by words first

Notice the frequency table treats `low`, `lower`, `lowest`, `newer`, `wider` as **separate words**, each with its own boundary. Merges only happen **within** a word — the algorithm never merges, say, the trailing `w` of `low` with the leading `n` of `newer`, even if you concatenated the whole corpus into one stream.

This is called **pre-tokenization**: split raw text on whitespace/punctuation into word chunks first, then run BPE merges *inside* each chunk independently. It's what classic BPE (and GPT-2's tokenizer) does. That's exactly the "Usually pre-tokenized" row in the comparison table from the lecture:

| Method | Whitespace handling |
|---|---|
| BPE | Usually pre-tokenized |
| WordPiece | Usually pre-tokenized |
| SentencePiece | Space becomes `▁` (no pre-split) |

## Is word-splitting required by the algorithm itself?

No — it's a design choice, not a mathematical necessity of "count pairs, merge most frequent." Two reasons people do it anyway:

1. **Prevents nonsense cross-word tokens** — without a word boundary, a frequent bigram like `"w "` + `"n"` at word joins could get merged just because it's common, producing tokens that straddle word boundaries meaninglessly.
2. **It's an English-centric assumption** — it silently relies on whitespace cleanly marking word boundaries.

## Where this assumption breaks (and gets removed)

This is exactly what the lecture flagged as SentencePiece's whole point:

> *"SentencePiece treats the raw input as a single stream of Unicode, spaces included, and represents each space explicitly with a marker (`▁`) rather than throwing whitespace away... it removes the hidden assumption that whitespace cleanly separates words. That assumption is an English habit, and it is exactly the assumption that breaks for many Indic scripts, where word boundaries are not marked the way they are in English."*

So:
```
"the cat" → pre-tokenize on space → ["the", "cat"] → run BPE inside each
```
vs. SentencePiece:
```
"the cat" → "▁the▁cat"  (one continuous stream, space is just another character)
→ BPE/Unigram merges run over the whole stream, no hard word boundary at all
```

For your assignment (Hindi/Telugu/Sanskrit especially), this matters directly — those scripts don't always have clean whitespace-delimited words the way English does, so a naive "split on spaces first" pre-tokenizer can be a worse fit than SentencePiece's space-as-character approach.


## 4. Encoding algorithm (the part the widget got wrong)

To tokenize brand-new text, you do **not** apply merges left-to-right through the string. You replay the merge list in **rank order** — repeatedly find the pair *anywhere* in the current sequence with the lowest rank (earliest-learned), and merge that one first:

```

    ranks = {pair: i for i, pair in enumerate(merges)}   # earlier = lower rank = higher priority
    symbols = list(byte_tokens(pre_token))

    while True:
        # find the adjacent pair with the LOWEST rank present in this sequence
        pairs = adjacent_pairs(symbols)
        candidate = min(pairs, key=lambda p: ranks.get(p, inf))
        if candidate not in ranks:
            break   # no known merge applies anymore
        symbols = merge_pair(symbols, candidate)

    return symbols
```

This matters because a later part of the string might contain an *earlier-learned* (higher-priority) merge than one earlier in the string — naive left-to-right scanning gets this wrong. Rank-based selection is what makes encoding deterministic and consistent with training.

```
   - sequence := corpus represented as a list of current symbols
     (initially just the base symbols, in original order, with no boundaries removed)

2. REPEAT until len(vocabulary) == V (or no pairs remain):

      - pair_counts := empty map
      - for every position i in sequence (except the last):
            pair := (symbol at i, symbol at i+1)
            pair_counts[pair] += 1
      - (this counts pairs wherever they occur in the sequence, using
         whatever boundary convention you've chosen — see note below)

   b. SELECT WINNER
      - best_pair := the pair with the highest count in pair_counts
      - break ties by a fixed, deterministic rule (e.g. first-seen order,
        or lexicographic) so training is reproducible

   c. MERGE
      - new_symbol := concatenation of best_pair's two symbols
      - replace every non-overlapping occurrence of best_pair in sequence
        with new_symbol (scan left to right, consuming both symbols each time)

   d. RECORD
      - append (best_pair -> new_symbol) to merge_rules, in order
      - add new_symbol to vocabulary

3. RETURN vocabulary, merge_rules
```

```
INPUT: new text, merge_rules (ordered), vocabulary
OUTPUT: sequence of tokens

1. sequence := new text represented as base symbols
   (same base unit used in training — bytes/codepoints)

2. for each rule (pair -> new_symbol) in merge_rules, IN ORDER:
       scan sequence left to right
       wherever the two symbols of `pair` appear adjacent,
       replace them with new_symbol
       (do this for every rule, one at a time, never skipping order)

3. return sequence  (this is the final list of tokens)
```

## Breaking the corpus into symbols — the options

This is the "step 0" alphabet choice, and it's not a free choice — it determines correctness for multilingual text. Three real options, in increasing order of robustness:

### 1. Character-level (naive)
Split by Unicode **grapheme clusters** — i.e. what a human perceives as "one visible character."

```
"नमस्ते" → ["न", "म", "स", "्", "त", "े"]  (or however the renderer groups it)
```

**Problem:** ambiguous and inconsistent. As covered in the lecture, a Devanagari conjunct like `क्ष` is visually one glyph but is stored as multiple Unicode *codepoints* (`क + ् + ष`). "Character" isn't even a well-defined boundary across scripts — grapheme segmentation rules differ per script and require a Unicode-aware library to get right at all.

### 2. Unicode codepoint-level (what most people mean by "character-level")
Split by individual Unicode **codepoints** — the actual atomic units Unicode assigns integers to.

```
"क्ष" → [U+0915 (क), U+094D (्, halant), U+0937 (ष)]   → 3 symbols, not 1
```

**Better than grapheme-splitting** because it's unambiguous and deterministic (Python's `list(string)` gives you this directly). **Still has a real problem for multilingual + limited vocab**: your base alphabet size = however many distinct codepoints exist across all languages in your corpus. English + Hindi + Telugu + Sanskrit easily needs hundreds of distinct codepoints just as your *starting* alphabet, before a single merge — and if the grader's held-out text contains a codepoint you never saw in training, you get an **unknown token** (BPE encoding breaks).

### 3. Byte-level (UTF-8 bytes) — the robust, correct choice
Encode the corpus to **UTF-8 bytes first**, then treat each byte (0–255) as a base symbol.

```
"क" → UTF-8 encode → bytes [0xE0, 0xA4, 0x95]  → 3 symbols
"A" → UTF-8 encode → byte  [0x41]              → 1 symbol
```

```
INPUT: corpus C (any Unicode text)
1. bytes ← UTF-8 encode(C)          # one deterministic, universal encoding
2. symbols ← the 256 possible byte values (0x00–0xFF)
3. sequence ← list of individual bytes from `bytes`
```

**Why this is the correct choice for your assignment:**
- **Fixed, tiny base alphabet (256 symbols)** regardless of how many languages/scripts you mix in — no per-language alphabet bookkeeping.
- **Zero unknown-token risk, ever.** Any string in any language decomposes fully into bytes 0–255. Worst case, a rare character just falls back to multiple raw-byte tokens instead of failing to tokenize at all. This directly satisfies the assignment's "UNK count: 0" requirement mentioned in your README.
- **Language-agnostic by construction** — you don't need separate logic for Devanagari conjuncts, halants, ZWJ/ZWNJ, Telugu vowel signs, etc. at the symbol-init stage. The BPE merge loop will naturally learn to fuse frequently co-occurring byte sequences (e.g. the 3 bytes of a common Devanagari consonant) into single tokens over training, because they *are* frequent adjacent pairs in the data.
- This is exactly what GPT-2/GPT-3/GPT-4's tokenizer (byte-level BPE) and Llama's byte-fallback SentencePiece do, precisely for this multilingual-robustness reason.

### Practical pseudocode difference

```
# Naive (codepoint-level) — risk of OOV codepoints, larger base alphabet
symbols = list(text)  # unicode chars

# Correct (byte-level) — fixed 256-symbol alphabet, no OOV ever
symbols = list(text.encode("utf-8"))  # ints 0-255
```

Everything else in the merge loop (count pairs, merge winner, record rule, repeat) is identical — only the **initial symbol representation** changes. Given your corpus mixes English, Hindi, Telugu, and Sanskrit, byte-level init is the correct starting point, not character-level.

## Breaking a corpus into symbols in Python

There are three common choices for the "base alphabet" — each with different implications for multilingual text like yours.

### 1. Character-level (Unicode codepoints)

```python
text = "the cat"
symbols = list(text)
# ['t', 'h', 'e', ' ', 'c', 'a', 't']
```

Simple, human-readable — but for Indic scripts, a single visual character (grapheme) like `क्ष` is actually **multiple Unicode codepoints**:

```python
word = "क्ष"
print(list(word))
# ['क', '्', 'ष']   <- 3 codepoints for what looks like 1 glyph
print(len(word))
# 3
```

This is the exact conjunct-consonant issue from the lecture — naive `list(text)` can split *inside* a grapheme cluster.

### 2. Byte-level (UTF-8 bytes) — what GPT-2/GPT-4-style BPE actually uses

```python
text = "the cat"
byte_seq = text.encode("utf-8")
symbols = [bytes([b]) for b in byte_seq]
# [b't', b'h', b'e', b' ', b'c', b'a', b't']
```

For non-ASCII text, each character can span multiple bytes:

```python
word = "क्ष"
b = word.encode("utf-8")
print(b)
# b'\xe0\xa4\x95\xe0\xa5\x8d\xe0\xa4\xb7'
print(len(b))
# 9 bytes (3 codepoints × 3 bytes each, Devanagari is in the 3-byte UTF-8 range)
symbols = [bytes([x]) for x in b]
```

**Why byte-level is the standard choice:** exactly 256 possible base symbols, guaranteed — every possible input (any language, emoji, malformed text) decomposes fully to bytes, so there's **never an unknown/OOV token**. This is what GPT-2 uses via `bytes_to_unicode()` (remaps the 256 byte values to printable Unicode chars purely so merge rules are human-readable in the vocab file).

### 3. Grapheme-cluster level (best for Indic scripts specifically)

Use `regex` (not stdlib `re`) with `\X` to split on **user-perceived characters** rather than raw codepoints — this respects conjuncts/matras as atomic units:

```python
import regex  # pip install regex — stdlib `re` does NOT support \X

word = "क्ष"
graphemes = regex.findall(r'\X', word)
print(graphemes)
# ['क्ष']   <- one grapheme cluster, kept intact
```

```python
word2 = "शक्ति"
print(regex.findall(r'\X', word2))
# ['श', 'क्ति']   (conjunct क् + ति stays fused as a cluster)
```

This directly avoids the "arbitrary split inside a conjunct" problem the lecture warned about (`शक | ् | ति`).

### Practical recommendation for your assignment

```python
import regex

def to_symbols(text: str, mode: str = "byte") -> list:
    if mode == "byte":
        return [bytes([b]) for b in text.encode("utf-8")]
    elif mode == "char":
        return list(text)
    elif mode == "grapheme":
        return regex.findall(r'\X', text)
```

## Creating the new symbol and doing the merge in Python

**New symbol** = just concatenate the two pieces (works for strings or bytes):

```python
new_symbol = pair[0] + pair[1]
```

**Non-overlapping left-to-right replacement** — you can't use `str.replace()` or a regex sub blindly here, because your `sequence` is a *list of symbols*, not a raw string, and you need index-aware, non-overlapping scanning. The idiomatic way:

```python
def merge_pair(sequence, pair, new_symbol):
    result = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(sequence):
        if i < len(sequence) - 1 and (sequence[i], sequence[i+1]) == pair:
            result.append(new_symbol)
            i += 2          # skip both merged symbols — this is the "non-overlapping" part
        else:
            result.append(sequence[i])
            i += 1
    return result
```

- `i += 2` after a match is what enforces **non-overlapping, continue-past-the-merge** scanning (so `a a a` with rule `a+a→aa` becomes `[aa, a]`, not `[a, aa]` or an infinite re-merge).

## Creating and replacing a merged symbol — the mechanics

### The sequence representation
Keep the corpus as a **list of symbols** (strings), not a raw string. This matters because after merges, a "symbol" like `lo` is 2 characters but must be treated as **one indivisible unit** going forward.

```python
sequence = ['l', 'o', 'w']   # not the string "low"
```

### Creating the new symbol
Just concatenate the two symbols in the winning pair — no magic, string concatenation:

```python
best_pair = ('l', 'o')
new_symbol = best_pair[0] + best_pair[1]   # 'lo'
```

### Replacing occurrences — left-to-right, non-overlapping scan

This is the part that actually matters for correctness. You **cannot** use a naive `str.replace()` or regex substitution on a joined string, because:
1. Symbols can be multi-character already (e.g. merging `lo` with `w` later), so you need to match whole *list elements*, not substrings.
2. You must advance the scan pointer past a merged token so it's not re-matched by the same or an overlapping pair.

The actual technique — walk the list with an index, and whenever you see the pair adjacent, splice it into one element and **jump the pointer past it**:

```python
i = 0
new_sequence = []
while i < len(sequence):
    if i < len(sequence) - 1 and (sequence[i], sequence[i+1]) == best_pair:
        new_sequence.append(new_symbol)
        i += 2          # skip both consumed symbols — this is the "non-overlapping" part
    else:
        new_sequence.append(sequence[i])
        i += 1
sequence = new_sequence
```

**Why `i += 2` and not `i += 1`:** if you only advanced by 1, a pattern like `('a','a','a')` with merge rule `a+a→aa` could re-trigger overlapping — you'd want deterministic behavior (e.g. `aa, a` not `a, aa`), and jumping past the whole consumed pair is what guarantees that.

### Applying this across the whole corpus

You do this same replace-pass over **every word/sequence in your corpus** that contains the pair, not just one instance — and you do it once per merge step, since merging changes what "adjacent" means for the next round of counting.

### At the vocab level

```python
vocab.add(new_symbol)
merges.append((best_pair, new_symbol))
```

That's the entire mechanical core: concatenate strings for `new_symbol`, then a single linear list-scan with an index that jumps by 2 on a match — no regex, no recursion, just careful pointer arithmetic so merges are non-overlapping and deterministic.

Whatever wins this is a single character that's *already* a single unit in your vocab. ## What the merges list actually is

```
vocab   = the SET of tokens that exist               {l, o, w, e, r, lo, low, ...}
merges  = the ORDERED SEQUENCE of rules to derive them [ (l,o)→lo, (lo,w)→low, ... ]
```

## Why vocab alone is useless for tokenizing anything new

You trained on `"low lower lowest flow"` and got vocab `{lo, low, ' low', ...}`. Now someone hands you a brand new word never seen in training: `"slower"`.

```
sequence = ['s', 'l', 'o', 'w', 'e', 'r']
```

**Question: how do you turn this into tokens using only `vocab` (a set, no order)?**

You can't just "look for the longest matching substring greedily" reliably — that's a *different* algorithm (more like WordPiece-style greedy matching), not BPE. BPE's actual contract is: **replay the exact merges, in the exact order they were learned**, because later merges assume earlier merges already happened.

```
merges = [
  1. (l, o)   -> lo
  2. (lo, w)  -> low
  3. (' ', low) -> ' low'
]

apply to "slower":
  start:            s l o w e r
  rule 1 (l+o->lo): s lo w e r        <- matches, apply
  rule 2 (lo+w->low): s low e r       <- matches, apply
  rule 3 (' '+low->' low'): no match  <- 's' precedes 'low', not a space; skip

  final: ['s', 'low', 'e', 'r']
```

This only works because you replayed rules **in the order they were discovered**. If you'd only had the `vocab` set `{lo, low, ' low', s, e, r, ...}` with no order, you'd have no principled way to decide: do I look for `low` first, or `lo` first, or `' low'` first? Different orders give different, potentially wrong, segmentations — and worse, some merges are *only valid because an earlier merge already fired* (rule 3 needs `low` to already exist as one unit before it can even check `' '+low`).

It's a **training** function, not a tokenizer. Better names:

```
INPUT:  new text T

RETURN ids
```

```
merges tells you:  WHICH characters to fuse, and in what order       (produces token strings)
vocab   tells you:  WHAT integer id each resulting token string maps to   (produces the final ids)
```

They're used **sequentially**, not simultaneously — merges first transforms raw text into a sequence of token *strings*, then vocab converts those strings into integer *ids* the model actually consumes.

def merge(seq: list[str], sym1: str, sym2) -> MergeResult:

Your function signature promises `MergeResult`, and every other path returns `MergeResult(updated_seq=..., created_symbol=...)`. But when there's no match, it silently returns a bare `list[str]` instead.

Proof:

**Why this hasn't crashed yet:** in your current `train_bpe`, the winning pair from `Counter.most_common(1)` is *always* a pair that actually exists in `sequence` (by construction — you're counting real pairs), so this no-match branch never actually fires during training. It's dead code today, but it's a landmine.

**When it'll haunt you:** the moment you write `encode()` and replay a merge rule on **new text** where that particular pair might legitimately not be present (e.g. the `"slower"` example from earlier — rule 3 doesn't match there). Your `encode()` loop will do:

```python
sequence, symbol = merge_res.updated_seq, merge_res.created_symbol
```

and crash with `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'updated_seq'` the instant a merge rule doesn't apply — which will happen on almost every real piece of unseen text.

## The idea: don't rebuild counts from scratch — update incrementally

Right now:
```
every iteration:
    pairs = zip(sequence[:-1], sequence[1:])   # O(n) full rescan
    Counter(pairs).most_common(1)               # O(n) full recount
```

That's wasteful because **merging one pair only changes counts in a tiny neighborhood** — everywhere else in the sequence, adjacency is untouched.

## What actually changes after a merge

```
before merge, sequence:  ... X  a  b  Y ...
merging pair (a, b) -> ab

after merge:              ... X  ab  Y ...
```

Only the pairs **touching** the merge site are affected:
```
removed:  (X, a), (a, b), (b, Y)
added:    (X, ab), (ab, Y)
```

Everywhere else in the sequence, pair counts are **identical to before**. You don't need to recount them.

## The structure that makes this fast

```
1. pair_counts = Counter(...)      built ONCE, full O(n) pass, at the very start

2. positions[pair] = set of indices where this pair currently occurs
                      (so you know WHERE to look, not scan everything)

3. a max-heap (or priority queue) keyed by count
   -> gives you the top pair in O(log n) instead of O(n) scan

4. on each merge:
   - look up positions[best_pair]           # only these spots need updating
   - for each occurrence, update ONLY the neighboring pairs:
       decrement count of (left_neighbor, a) and (b, right_neighbor)
       increment count of (left_neighbor, ab) and (ab, right_neighbor)
   - push updated counts onto the heap
   - pop from heap to get next top pair (may need "lazy deletion":
     if a popped entry's count doesn't match current pair_counts, it's stale — discard and pop again)
```

## Why "lazy deletion" on the heap

You can't easily *decrease* a specific entry's priority in a standard heap. So instead:
```
- never delete/update heap entries in place
- just push a NEW entry whenever a count changes
- when popping the max, check: does this entry's stored count match pair_counts[pair] right now?
    if yes -> it's valid, use it
    if no  -> it's stale (superseded by a later push), discard and pop again
```

## Net effect

```
current approach:  O(n) per merge  x  total merges  = O(n × merges)
incremental heap:  O(log n) per pop + O(k log n) per merge to update k affected pairs
                    where k = occurrences of the merged pair (usually k << n)
```

For your real corpus (30k+ words, 2500 merges), this is the difference between a fast training run and one that visibly crawls.

This is genuinely the standard technique — it's how production BPE trainers (Hugging Face `tokenizers`, sentencepiece, original subword-nmt) actually implement training. Confirms it exactly.

## What `Counter.most_common(1)` actually does

```
n=None case:   sorted(self.items(), ...)         O(n log n) every call
n=1 case:      heapq.nlargest(1, self.items())   still O(n) every call
               (nlargest builds/scans over ALL items each time — it does not
                remember anything between calls)
```

**There is no persistent heap inside `Counter`.** Every call to `.most_common(n)` starts from scratch, scanning the *entire* dict, whether you call it once or a thousand times. Updating `counter[key] += 1` is cheap (O(1) dict update), but that update buys you nothing toward finding the max faster — you still pay full-scan cost the next time you ask "what's the top pair."

## What you'd need instead: build your own heap alongside the Counter

```
counter[pair] += delta         # O(1) — keep this, it's fine and necessary

heapq.heappush(heap, (-count, pair))    # push a NEW entry whenever count changes
                                          # (negative because heapq is min-heap only)

# to get current max:
while heap:
    neg_count, pair = heapq.heappop(heap)
    if -neg_count == counter[pair]:      # validate against ground truth
        best_pair = pair
        break
    # else: stale entry (count changed since this was pushed) -> discard, loop continues
```

This is exactly the **lazy deletion** pattern from before — `Counter` stays your source of truth for "what is the count right now," and a separate `heapq` list gives you fast max-retrieval, tolerating the fact that old, now-invalid entries just get skipped when popped.

So to directly answer: `Counter` alone cannot give you O(log n) max-lookup — you must pair it with an explicit `heapq` (or another priority-queue structure) yourself; Python's stdlib doesn't fuse the two for you.

## Production BPE = incremental heap (what we discussed) + one more big lever: dedupe words first

### The biggest lever: don't count over the raw corpus at all — count over unique word types

```
naive:      scan every character position in the ENTIRE corpus     O(corpus length)
production: split into words once, DEDUPE identical words,
            keep {word: frequency}                                  O(unique word types)
```

Example: your English page has ~30,789 words but only ~7,015 *unique* words. Every production BPE trainer (original subword-nmt, Hugging Face `tokenizers`, SentencePiece) works over this deduped `{word: count}` map, not the raw token stream. This alone can shrink the working set by 4-10x before any heap trickery.

```
word_counts = {
    ('l','o','w'): 5,
    ('l','o','w','e','r'): 2,
    ('l','o','w','e','s','t'): 1,
    ...
}
```

Pair counts are computed **once**, weighted by each word's frequency — matches exactly what the lecture's original toy example did (`low×5` etc.), which is itself modeling this real technique, not simplifying it away.

### Then: incremental heap + inverted index (what we already covered), but scoped to word types

```
pair_counts:  {pair: total weighted count}           (built once, O(unique words))
where:        {pair: set of word-type indices
                     where this pair currently occurs}   <- inverted index

heap:         max-heap of (count, pair), with lazy deletion
```

On each merge of `best_pair`:
```
1. look up where[best_pair]           -> only these word types are affected
                                          (not the whole corpus, not even all unique words)
2. for each affected word:
     merge best_pair inside that one word's symbol tuple
     decrement counts for the pairs that existed around the merge site
     increment counts for the pairs newly created around the merge site
     (each occurrence only touches its own tiny local neighborhood,
      weighted by that word's frequency)
3. push updated (count, pair) entries onto heap
4. pop heap, skip stale entries (count mismatch vs pair_counts), until a valid top pair is found
```

### Why this combination matters

```
work per merge  ≈  O(occurrences of best_pair)  ×  O(word length near merge site)
                    NOT O(entire corpus)
```

Since `where[pair]` tells you exactly which words to touch, a merge that only appears in, say, 40 unique word types costs you work proportional to 40, not to 30,789 (or however large the corpus is).

### What real implementations look like, concretely

- **subword-nmt** (original Sennrich reference implementation): dedupes into `{word: freq}`, uses a priority queue over pairs with an index tracking which words contain each pair, updates only affected words per merge.
- **Hugging Face `tokenizers`** (Rust, what most people actually train with today): same shape — word-frequency table + a max-heap (`BinaryHeap` in Rust) + a "pairs to recompute" set touched only by the current merge's affected words, all written for speed since it's compiled.
- **SentencePiece**: different algorithm family for Unigram mode, but its BPE mode follows the same dedup + incremental-count principle.

### How this maps onto your code

```
your current tokenizer/train_bpe:  operates on `sequence = list(txt)`  (full raw text, no word split)

production style:                   pre-tokenize -> dedupe into {word_tuple: freq}
                                     -> build pair_counts weighted by freq
                                     -> heap + inverted index for incremental updates
```

This is also exactly the thing from a few turns ago about word-splitting being a *pre-tokenization convention*, not a BPE requirement — here's the concrete payoff for **why** production trainers still do it: it turns "count over millions of characters" into "count over thousands of unique word types," which is the single biggest speed win before you even add the heap.

316:                        if script_of_pair(p[0], p[1])
317:                        in (group, "NUM", "OTHER")
318:                        or (group == "DEV" and script_of_pair(p[0], p[1]) == "DEV")
319:                    ]
320:                    seen = set()
321:                    pool = []
322:                    for p in pref[: candidate_k // 2] + candidates:
323:                        if p not in seen:
324:                            seen.add(p)
325:                            pool.append(p)
326:                    candidates = pool
327:                if not candidates:
328:                    break
329:                Tf = current_T()
330:                Xf = current_X(Tf)
331:                worst_lang = max(LANGS, key=lambda l: Xf[l])
332:                best_key = None
333:                for pair in candidates:
334:                    # merge removes one token per occurrence of the pair
335:                    T2 = {l: Tf[l] - pair_lang[pair][l] for l in LANGS}
336:                    X2 = current_X(T2)
337:                    key = (
338:                        gap_of(X2),
339:                        max(X2.values()),
340:                        -pair_w[pair],
341:                        -pair_lang[pair][worst_lang],
342:                    )
343:                    if best_key is None or key < best_key:
344:                        best_key = key
345:                        best = pair
346:
347:            if best is None:
348:                break
349:            if pair_w[best] < min_freq and sum(pair_lang[best].values()) < 1:
350:                break
351:
352:            apply_merge(best)
353:            merges_done += 1
354:            if verbose and (merges_done % 250 == 0 or merges_done <= 2):
355:                T = current_T()
356:                X = current_X(T)
357:                sg = script_of_pair(best[0], best[1])
358:                print(
359:                    f"  merge {merges_done}: {best[0]!r}+{best[1]!r} "
360:                    f"script={sg} gap={gap_of(X):.4f} "
361:                    f"X=[{', '.join(f'{X[l]:.3f}' for l in LANGS)}]"
362:                )
363:
364:        if verbose:
365:            T = current_T()
366:            X = current_X(T)
367:            print(
368:                f"  after {merges_done} merges vocab={len(self.vocab)} "
369:                f"gap={gap_of(X):.4f}"
370:            )
371:
372:        # Whole-word fill: under-resourced first so TE/SA are not starved
373:        if whole_word_fill:
374:            remaining = MAX_VOCAB - len(self.vocab)
375:            alloc = {l: int(remaining * budget[l]) for l in LANGS}
376:            alloc["EN"] += remaining - sum(alloc.values())
377:            per_lang = {
378:                l: sorted(lang_word_freq[l].items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])
379:                for l in LANGS
380:            }
381:            added_w = {l: 0 for l in LANGS}
382:            for l in ("SA", "TE", "HI", "EN"):
383:                for w, _c in per_lang[l]:
384:                    if len(self.vocab) >= MAX_VOCAB:
385:                        break
386:                    if added_w[l] >= int(alloc[l] * 1.8) and any(
387:                        added_w[o] < alloc[o] for o in LANGS if o != l
388:                    ):
389:                        continue
390:                    if w not in self.vocab and self._add(w):
391:                        self.word_tokens.add(w)
392:                        added_w[l] += 1
393:            # dump any remaining unique words (shared multiling forms)
394:            combined = Counter()
395:            for l in LANGS:
396:                combined.update(lang_word_freq[l])
397:            for w, _c in combined.most_common():
398:                if len(self.vocab) >= MAX_VOCAB:
399:                    break
400:                if w not in self.vocab and self._add(w):
401:                    self.word_tokens.add(w)
402:            if verbose:
403:                print(
404:                    f"  whole-words by_lang={added_w} vocab={len(self.vocab)}"
405:                )
406:
407:        # Gap-safe phrase fill: only accept phrases that do not enlarge gap
408:        if phrase_fill and len(self.vocab) < MAX_VOCAB:
409:            self._gap_safe_phrases(
410:                word_lists, D, budget, phrase_max_n, verbose=verbose
411:            )
412:
413:        self._rebuild_maps()
414:        elapsed = time.time() - t0
415:        if verbose:
416:            print(
417:                f"  done in {elapsed:.1f}s vocab={len(self.vocab)} "
418:                f"merges={len(self.merges)} phrases={len(self.phrase_tokens)}"
419:            )
420:        return {
421:            "merges": merges_done,
422:            "vocab_size": len(self.vocab),
423:            "temperature": temperature,
424:            "budget": budget,
425:            "mult": mult,
426:            "variant": variant,
427:            "elapsed_s": elapsed,
428:        }

430:    def _gap_safe_phrases(
431:        self,
432:        word_lists: Dict[str, List[str]],
433:        D: Dict[str, float],
434:        budget: Dict[str, float],
435:        phrase_max_n: int,
436:        verbose: bool = True,
437:    ) -> None:
438:        """Add phrase tokens only when estimated gap does not grow.
439:
440:        Savings use non-overlapping L2R match counts (fast); under whole-word
441:        vocab this closely matches encode_words.
442:        """
443:        _ = budget
444:
445:        def ngram_save(words: List[str], ph: str) -> int:
446:            ps = ph.split()
447:            nn = len(ps)
448:            if nn < 2:
449:                return 0
450:            c = 0
451:            i = 0
452:            while i <= len(words) - nn:
453:                if words[i : i + nn] == ps:
454:                    c += 1
455:                    i += nn
456:                else:
457:                    i += 1
458:            return (nn - 1) * c
459:
460:        T = {l: float(len(self.encode_words(word_lists[l]))) for l in LANGS}
461:        X = {l: T[l] / D[l] for l in LANGS}
462:        gap = max(X.values()) - min(X.values())
463:
464:        cands: Dict[str, List[Tuple[str, int, int]]] = {}
465:        for l in LANGS:
466:            items = []
467:            w = word_lists[l]
468:            for n in range(2, phrase_max_n + 1):
469:                pc: Counter = Counter()
470:                for i in range(len(w) - n + 1):
471:                    pc[" ".join(w[i : i + n])] += 1
472:                for ph, f in pc.items():
473:                    if f >= 1:
474:                        items.append((ph, n, f))
475:            items.sort(key=lambda x: -((x[1] - 1) * x[2]))
476:            cands[l] = items[:4000]
477:        ptr = {l: 0 for l in LANGS}
478:        added = 0
479:        stagnant = 0
480:        while len(self.vocab) < MAX_VOCAB and stagnant < 4:
481:            worst = max(LANGS, key=lambda l: X[l])
482:            accepted = False
483:            for focus in [worst] + [l for l in LANGS if l != worst]:
484:                trials = 0
485:                while ptr[focus] < len(cands[focus]) and trials < 80:
486:                    ph, n, f = cands[focus][ptr[focus]]
487:                    ptr[focus] += 1
488:                    trials += 1
489:                    tok = "▁" + ph.replace(" ", "▁")
490:                    if ph in self.phrase_tokens or tok in self.vocab:
491:                        continue
492:                    save = {l: ngram_save(word_lists[l], ph) for l in LANGS}
493:                    if all(v == 0 for v in save.values()):
494:                        continue
495:                    T2 = {l: T[l] - save[l] for l in LANGS}
496:                    X2 = {l: T2[l] / D[l] for l in LANGS}
497:                    gap2 = max(X2.values()) - min(X2.values())
498:                    if gap2 <= gap + 1e-15:
499:                        if not self._add(tok):
500:                            return
501:                        self.phrase_tokens[ph] = tok
502:                        gap = gap2
503:                        X = X2
504:                        T = T2
505:                        added += 1
506:                        accepted = True
507:                        stagnant = 0
508:                        break
509:                if accepted:
510:                    break
511:            if not accepted:
512:                stagnant += 1
513:        if verbose:
514:            T = {l: float(len(self.encode_words(word_lists[l]))) for l in LANGS}
515:            X = {l: T[l] / D[l] for l in LANGS}
516:            gap = max(X.values()) - min(X.values())
517:            print(
518:                f"  gap-safe phrases added={added} vocab={len(self.vocab)} "
519:                f"gap={gap:.8f} X=[{', '.join(f'{X[l]:.4f}' for l in LANGS)}]"
520:            )

523:    def _bpe_word(self, word: str) -> List[str]:
524:        if word in self.vocab and len(word) > 1:
525:            return [word]
526:        if len(word) == 1:
527:            return [word if word in self.vocab else "<UNK>"]
528:        symbols = list(word)
529:        ranks = self._ranks
530:        if not ranks:
531:            return [c if c in self.vocab else "<UNK>" for c in symbols]
532:        while True:
533:            min_rank = None
534:            min_i = None
535:            for i in range(len(symbols) - 1):
536:                pair = (symbols[i], symbols[i + 1])
537:                r = ranks.get(pair)
538:                if r is not None and (min_rank is None or r < min_rank):
539:                    min_rank = r
540:                    min_i = i
541:            if min_i is None:
542:                break
543:            a, b = symbols[min_i], symbols[min_i + 1]
544:            symbols = symbols[:min_i] + [a + b] + symbols[min_i + 2 :]
545:        out = []
546:        for s in symbols:
547:            if s in self.vocab:
548:                out.append(s)
549:            else:
550:                for c in s:
551:                    out.append(c if c in self.vocab else "<UNK>")
552:        return out

554:    def encode_words(self, words: List[str]) -> List[str]:
555:        tokens: List[str] = []
556:        i = 0
557:        n = len(words)
558:        max_n = 1
559:        if self.phrase_tokens:
560:            max_n = max(len(p.split()) for p in self.phrase_tokens)
561:        while i < n:
562:            matched = False
563:            if self.phrase_tokens:
564:                for L in range(min(max_n, n - i), 1, -1):
565:                    ph = " ".join(words[i : i + L])
566:                    if ph in self.phrase_tokens:
567:                        tokens.append(self.phrase_tokens[ph])
568:                        i += L
569:                        matched = True
570:                        break
571:            if matched:
572:                continue
573:            w = words[i]
574:            if w in self.vocab:
575:                tokens.append(w)
576:            else:
577:                tokens.extend(self._bpe_word(w))
578:            i += 1
579:        return tokens

582:        return self.encode_words(extract_words(text))

You're trying to avoid **re-counting the exact same adjacent-pair pattern over and over** when it comes from the exact same word, appearing many times in the corpus.

## Concretely, what repeats today

```
en_txt contains "India" roughly 500+ times (it's the India Wikipedia page)

each occurrence of "India" as characters: ['I','n','d','i','a']
pairs inside it: (I,n), (n,d), (d,i), (i,a)   <- IDENTICAL every single time
```

Right now, your flat-sequence approach walks past every one of those ~500 occurrences separately and tallies `(I,n)`, `(n,d)`, `(d,i)`, `(i,a)` fresh, one at a time, 500 times over — even though the answer ("these 4 pairs, in this exact pattern") is exactly the same every time.

## What splitting into words + deduping lets you memoize

```
instead of counting 500 separate physical occurrences...

count ONCE:  word "India" -> appears 500 times (just a frequency number)
then compute pairs ONCE for "India": (I,n),(n,d),(d,i),(i,a)
then MULTIPLY each pair's count by 500 (the word's frequency)
```

So the **pattern-discovery work** (walking the 5 characters, listing adjacent pairs) happens once per *unique* word, not once per *occurrence* of that word. The frequency multiplier substitutes for re-scanning.

## Why this is a memoization in the classic sense

```
memoization = cache the result of an expensive computation, keyed by input,
              so repeated identical inputs reuse the cached result instead
              of recomputing

here:
    input      = a unique word (e.g. "India")
    expensive
    computation = decompose into pairs
    "cache key" = the word string itself
    "cached
    result"     = the list of internal pairs for that word

repeated occurrences of the SAME word never redo the decomposition —
they just contribute their count as a multiplier on the already-known pairs
```

```
before: work scales with TOTAL word occurrences  (~30,789 for English)
after:  work scales with UNIQUE word types only   (~7,015 for English)
```

## Why it's an acceptable tradeoff, not a bug

Classic BPE (as used in GPT-2, RoBERTa, etc.) makes this exact choice deliberately: **pre-tokenize into words first, merge only within each word.** This isn't a limitation people are stuck with — it's a design decision with real justification.

```

    "India is" — even if "a" (end of India) + " " (space) is globally
    frequent, you'd never form that as a token spanning two words

    - tokens stay semantically coherent (a token is always part of
      ONE word, never a meaningless straddle across two unrelated words)
    - dramatically fewer pairs to ever consider (word-internal only)
    - the word-frequency dedup trick becomes possible (this is WHY
      classic BPE splits on words — it's what unlocks the memoization
      we discussed)
```

## The caveat: word boundary ≠ throwing away the space entirely

You can't just drop the space and pretend words are independent chunks with no boundary information at all — otherwise detokenization (turning tokens back into readable text) becomes ambiguous: was there a space between these two words or not?

This is exactly why SentencePiece keeps the space as an **explicit marker** (`▁`) attached to the start of a word, rather than a shareable, mergeable character floating between two words:

```
"India is"  ->  "▁India▁is"
splits: {"▁India": [...], "▁is": [...]}

the ▁ still marks "there was a space here" — but it belongs to
ONE word (the one it prefixes), so it can still participate in
merges WITHIN that word (e.g. ▁+I -> ▁I), never across into the
previous word's trailing characters
```

## Where this leaves you

```
your current flat-sequence version:  allows genuinely cross-word merges
                                      (e.g. ' '+'low' from your earlier trace)
                                      — unusual, not "wrong" but non-standard

word-dedup version (if you switch):  never merges across words
                                      — this is the STANDARD behavior,
                                      matches how production BPE works,
                                      and is what unlocks the speed benefit
```

So yes — dropping cross-word/cross-subword merges is not just "okay," it's the conventional, expected behavior of BPE as it's actually implemented in practice. Your current toy example forming `(' ', 'low')` was actually the non-standard case, not the other way around.

## Yes, exactly — pairs are formed **within** each word, and this happens **once per unique word**, not once per occurrence.

## Concretely

```
corpus (raw):  "low lower lowest flow"

STEP 1 — split into words, dedupe:
    word_freq = {"low": 1, "lower": 1, "lowest": 1, "flow": 1}
    (in this toy example all unique, so freq=1 each — the benefit
     shows up on YOUR real corpus where "India" repeats ~500 times,
     "the" repeats thousands of times, etc.)

STEP 2 — represent each unique word as its own character list:
    splits = {
        "low":    ['l','o','w'],
        "lower":  ['l','o','w','e','r'],
        "lowest": ['l','o','w','e','s','t'],
        "flow":   ['f','l','o','w'],
    }

STEP 3 — for EACH unique word, separately, form its INTERNAL adjacent pairs:
    "low"    -> (l,o), (o,w)
    "lower"  -> (l,o), (o,w), (w,e), (e,r)
    "lowest" -> (l,o), (o,w), (w,e), (e,s), (s,t)
    "flow"   -> (f,l), (l,o), (o,w)

    (notice: NO pair ever crosses from one word's dict entry into
     another's — "flow"'s trailing 'w' is never paired with "low"'s
     leading 'l', even though they're both in `splits`)

STEP 4 — aggregate, weighted by each word's frequency:
    pair_counts = Counter()
    for word, chars in splits.items():
        f = word_freq[word]
        for i in range(len(chars)-1):
            pair_counts[(chars[i], chars[i+1])] += f
```

## The key mechanical point

You compute the pair list **once per unique word** (not once per occurrence in the raw text) — then that word's contribution to the global tally gets multiplied by how many times it actually appeared. Two different words never have their characters checked against each other for adjacency at all — the loop structure (`for word in splits`, then `for i in range(len(chars)-1)` inside) makes cross-word pairing structurally impossible, since `i+1` never goes past the end of that one word's own character list.

That's the full mechanism — same idea as your earlier `bkHC` cell's `zip(sequence[:-1], sequence[1:]))`, just applied **per-word** instead of across the whole flattened text.

## The optimization: incremental updates instead of recount-from-scratch

We touched this earlier (the heap discussion) — here's how it specifically plugs into the word-based `splits` structure you just walked through.

## The problem with recounting every iteration

```python
# what you'd naively do each merge:
pair_counts = Counter()
for word, chars in splits.items():        # loop ALL 7,015 unique words
    for i in range(len(chars)-1):
        pair_counts[(chars[i], chars[i+1])] += word_freq[word]
```

Even with word-dedup, this still redoes the **entire** 7,015-word scan every single merge iteration — most of those words are completely unaffected by the merge you just did.

## What production BPE does instead: track which pairs live in which words

```
inverted_index: pair -> set of words that currently contain this pair

e.g. inverted_index[('l','o')] = {"low", "lower", "lowest", "flow"}
```

Built **once**, at the start, alongside the first full pair count.

## The incremental update, after each merge

When you merge `best_pair = (a, b)` into `ab`:

```
1. look up ONLY the words affected:
       affected_words = inverted_index[best_pair]
       (e.g. only 4 words, not all 7,015)

2. for EACH affected word only:
       find where (a,b) occurs in that word's symbol list
       BEFORE merging, note its neighbors:
           left  = the symbol just before this occurrence (if any)
           right = the symbol just after this occurrence (if any)

       decrement pair_counts for the pairs that will DISAPPEAR:
           (left, a)  -= word_freq[word]     (if left exists)
           (a, b)     -= word_freq[word]     (this pair itself, being consumed)
           (b, right) -= word_freq[word]     (if right exists)

       apply the merge in that word (your merge() function, per-word)

       increment pair_counts for the pairs that get CREATED:
           (left, ab)  += word_freq[word]    (if left exists)
           (ab, right) += word_freq[word]    (if right exists)

       update inverted_index: remove word from index[(a,b)],
       add word to index[(left,ab)] and index[(ab,right)] as needed

3. push these updated counts onto a heap (lazy deletion, as discussed)
   to find the NEXT best pair in O(log n) instead of a fresh O(words) scan
```

## Why this is fast

```
cost per merge  ≈  O(number of words containing the winning pair)
                    NOT O(all unique words)
```

If `('l','o')` only appears in 4 out of 7,015 words, you do ~4 words' worth of work, not 7,015. Over ~2,500 merges, this compounds into a massive difference versus recounting everything every time.

## Summary of the full stack (all three layers combined)

```
layer 1 (dedup words):         O(all chars in corpus)  ->  O(unique words)
layer 2 (inverted index):      O(unique words) per merge -> O(words containing THIS pair)
layer 3 (heap w/ lazy delete): O(n) to find max -> O(log n) to find max
```

This exact combination (dedupe + inverted index + priority queue with lazy deletion) is what Hugging Face's Rust `tokenizers` library and the original `subword-nmt` reference implementation both do — it's the standard production recipe, not a novel technique.

## The bug: `heapify_max` mutates in-place and returns `None`

```python
max_heap = heapq.heapify_max([(cnt, item) for item, cnt in pair_counts.items()])
```

Same category of bug as `list.sort()` vs `sorted()`:

```
heapq.heapify(lst)       -> reorders lst IN PLACE, returns None
heapq.heapify_max(lst)   -> same: reorders IN PLACE, returns None

sorted(lst)              -> returns a NEW sorted list  (what you're expecting)
lst.sort()               -> sorts IN PLACE, returns None  (the gotcha you hit)
```

`heapify_max` follows the `list.sort()` convention, not the `sorted()` convention — it turns your list into a valid max-heap **in memory**, but the function itself always returns `None`. Assigning that `None` to `max_heap` is what wipes out your data.

## The fix

```python
max_heap = [(cnt, item) for item, cnt in pair_counts.items()]
heapq.heapify_max(max_heap)      # mutates max_heap in place, no assignment
print(f"{max_heap=}")             # now correctly populated
```

```python
words_set: set[str] = word_freq.elements()
```
